courses.title: Dancechamberdance
courses.description: This course will guide students through all elements of producing a collaborative performance event in a condensed timeline, including rehearsal scheduling, lighting design, stage management, event coordination, and publicity. Students will work to create interdisciplinary collaborations between music and dance. The class will be responsible for all production and design elements, mentored by the instructor, including the curation of, the designation of management roles among the group, and devising a name and poster for the final performance. Graduate Dance majors only; typically offered Fall

courses.title: The Development of Dance Music
courses.description: This course, designed for dancers, musicologists, performers, and conductors, will review selected choreographic literature and musical scores from the repertory of late nineteenth and twentieth century concert dance. We will examine a range of dance/music relationships through a variety of readings, choreographic and musical scores, and audio recordings. We will also study the works of choreographers, conductors, and composers who have helped to shape the field. Our examination of music from the dance repertory will reach beyond those works composed specifically for dance and will incorporate studies of Baroque, Court, and Social Dance forms. Graduate Dance majors only; instructor permission required; typically offered Winter

courses.title: Dance and Related Arts
courses.description: Dance students collaborate with composers, visual artists, videographers, etc. to create an evening-length happening/collage/performance. Graduate Dance majors only; instructor permission required; typically offered Fall

courses.title: Accompanying Movement
courses.description: In this course, musicians will learn how to accompany for kinesthetic, movement-based art forms through the study and analysis of western dance technique classes. Using both Modern Dance and Ballet Technique courses typically offered in the Department of Dance, musicians will observe and analyze the structure and content of the class, will research the specific genre of the class, and by observing the methods of communication used between instructor and dance student, instructor and musician, and dance student and musician, they will learn how to collaborate in a dance class. Throughout the term, the student will accompany individual combinations so that by the end of the term, they will be able to provide an appropriate standard of music for an entire class session. This will provide the musician with an entry into collaboration with movement-based art forms. Graduate Dance majors only; instructor permission required; typically offered Fall, Winter

courses.title: Thesis Performance
courses.description: Thesis Performance. Graduate Dance majors only; instructor permission required; typically offered Fall, Winter

courses.title: Thesis 1: Summer Research Project
courses.description: Between the first and second year of the Masters' program, students will undertake extensive research off-campus, conducting fieldwork and developing material for their Thesis. The Summer Research Project comprises three components: 1) a 1,000 word proposal articulating the aims, methodology, research context and questions of the project, and of their relevance to the students' subsequent Thesis and to the field (20%); 2) a minimum of 40 hours in the field' (50%); 3) a 15-minute presentation of results, to include audio-visual examples and/or a performative element, plus Q&A (30%). Prerequisite: DANCE 501 and 502 with a grade of C or better. Graduate Dance majors only; instructor permission required; typically offered Winter

courses.title: Dance History and Theory
courses.description: This course introduces students to historical concepts, theories and methodologies, and to the major dance historians of the 19th-20th centuries. The aim is to develop a critical awareness of the competing constructions of dance history and of the interplay between history and other disciplines within and beyond dance. Students will interrogate different approaches to reading and writing our dancing past through the use of selected case studies, spanning textual, visual, oral and performative histories. Prerequisite: DANCE 501 and 502 (B- or better). Graduate Dance majors only; instructor permission required; typically offered Fall

courses.title: Research in Action (RIA) 3: Problematizing Theory in Practice
courses.description: The overarching aim of this culminating Research in Action course is for students to draw together strands from all areas of learning; to make connections to their MFA Thesis; and to acquire complete set of skills for their next steps in dance, either as leading practitioners in the field or within academia. Prerequisite: DANCE 501 and 502 (B- or better). Graduate Dance majors only; instructor permission required; typically offered Winter

courses.title: Ballet
courses.description: This advanced ballet course addresses core concepts of technique, alignment, anatomically sound movement, and artistry. Emphasis will be placed on more challenging combinations of movements so that students can explore transitions, musicality, increased mental acuity to remember new and complex sequences, and the ability to process information both in the brain and in the body. Students are encouraged to dance in three dimensions and to develop their individual sense of artistry through the class material. They should demonstrate a more advanced mastery of these concepts than in their first year of study. Graduate Dance majors only; instructor permission required; typically offered Fall, Winter

courses.title: Contemporary Dance
courses.description: This course requires the advanced level student to research and integrate compositional and performance methods into a lively and productive practice of dance-making. Through daily practice in class and in written assignments, students will acquire a sophisticated comprehension of the ways in which the creative process is embedded in technique. This course will act as an experiential laboratory for improvisation, composition and performance, anchored by sound technical practice. The study and practice of improvisation will serve as tools for both creative work in composition and performance. Elements of personal history and philosophy will be examined and questioned as a means of distilling idiosyncratic material and formal, shapely, dynamic and coherent structures. Exploring individual movement vocabularies will serve to refine and expand our physical language as form and structure emerges. Graduate Dance majors only; instructor permission required; typically offered Fall, Winter, Spring

courses.title: World Dance
courses.description: This studio course explores a variety of nonwestern folkloric and classical dance forms, their socio-cultural framework, as well as historical contexts through studio practice, discussion and readings. The goal of these courses is to increase student knowledge of dance traditions outside North American, (and of selected Native American traditions), further their understanding of spatial, religious, social restrictions of these dance forms, analyze socio-historical and cultural context, as well as to identify commonalities and continuities across genres. Based on instructor availability, it may focus on the particular tradition or a variety across genres. Graduate Dance majors only; instructor permission required; typically offered Fall, Winter, Spring

courses.description: This course is designed for students who wish to undertake a performance or repertory project beyond the University of Michigan. The 'field' of study is determined by the student, as is the nature and scope of the project, in consultation with a designated advisor. Such a project can be undertaken locally, nationally or overseas, with the number of credit hours determined by the project's parameters, timescale and complexity. Graduate Dance majors only; instructor permission required; typically offered Fall, Winter, Spring, Summer

courses.title: Independent Study: Performance/Repertory
courses.description: This course is designed for students who wish to study one or more dance performance or repertory experiences in-depth. The nature of the investigation is student-designed and directed, in consultation with a designated advisor. Both methodology and outcomes can be either practice-based or follow more traditional scholarly forms, for example, a final research paper or conference presentation. Graduate Dance majors only; instructor permission required; typically offered Fall, Winter, Spring, Summer

courses.title: Graduate Studio
courses.description: This course creates a forum for graduate students to investigate and workshop ideas, movement studies, production elements and choreographic projects with their peers and instructor to further investigate the embodiment of their thesis project materials. The primary goal of this course is to learn how to formulate questions about the act and creation of new work. Incentive and critical feedback are provided in order to push expectations, foster creative risk-taking and to maximize students' talent as performers and dance makers. Studio practice is supported by video viewings, readings, and discussion. The course meets once a week for 3 hours with additional lab time for independent research and sketching of movement materials. Thesis chairs and committee members will be invited to periodic showings and discussions of the evolving materials, and the instructor will work with the students on creating agreements with their casts that serve the creative process. Graduate Dance majors only; instructor permission required; typically offered Fall

courses.title: Performance Improvisation 2
courses.description: This course offers students the chance to deepen their improvisation practice and return to and examine questions and processes that emerged in the first section. Second-year MFA students become leaders, instigators, and influential risk takers. This course introduces students to the practice of improvisation as a performing art. They will engage as artist, soloist, collaborator and, collectively, create a performance ensemble. Theory and practice will be combined through journaling, reading, writing a program note and a final paper. Multiple showings including off-site performances, throughout the term, allow for students to gain confidence and creative agency. Graduate Dance majors only; instructor permission required; typically offered Fall

The courses will differ thematically, dependent upon the teaching and research expertise of the instructor. Graduate Dance majors only; instructor permission required; typically offered Fall, Winter

courses.title: Screendance 2: Advanced Projects and Productions
courses.description: Building upon the editing and camera skills, and creative research acquired in 542 Screendance 1, (prerequisite), this course challenges the student to propose three projects ranging from work for the screen, work for gallery or installation, and work for integration into live performance. In collaboration with faculty advisors and chosen venue, the student will then select one proposed project for completion and final production. Students are strongly encouraged to submit work(s) to festivals and/or present finished work(s) to audiences in innovative formats. Graduate Dance majors only; instructor permission required; typically offered Winter

courses.title: Somatic Study
courses.description: Somatics is the study of the inter-relational process between awareness, biological function and environment, all three factors being understood as a synergistic whole. This course builds on the knowledge gained in 551. Experiential Anatomy and offers a survey of various theoretical approaches to somatic perspectives, dance and movement therapy, as well as selected contemporary aesthetic/creative-based theories of movement through the lens of somatics. Through lectures, discussions and experiential based explorations, students will gain new insights into their physical and mental beings and how best to use somatics as a tool in dance. Graduate Dance majors only; instructor permission required; typically offered Fall, Winter

courses.title: Reading and Writing Dance History
courses.description: This course examines the nature and purposes of history by interrogating a range of theories, practices and issues both from within and outside dance. Case studies will be used to enable students to engage critically with notions and schools of history, different constructions of dance and performance histories, multiple and/or conflicting interpretations and current debates. Students will analyze a range of written, oral, visual and electronic source materials and will be encouraged to develop independent arguments and offer alternative readings. Graduate Dance majors only; instructor permission required; typically offered Fall, Winter

courses.title: Dancing Diasporas
courses.description: Using a chronological and geographical approach, this course examines Africanist and Asian performance trends across the Americas in dance, music, and theater, tracing them from West and Central Africa through the African Diaspora in the Americas. Through film screenings, lectures, discussions and movement sessions, students will investigate the commonalities and aesthetics of these forms, as well as the socio-cultural conditions that contributed to their creation and evolution. Graduate Dance majors only; instructor permission required; typically offered Fall, Winter

courses.title: Designing for Dance
courses.description: This course examines the art and practices of designing costumes, scenery and lighting for dance. Students assume the role of sole designer for one choreographic work, working from a rehearsal video and choreographer's notes. Each assignment is assessed through a design presentation to the class and the choreographer. For the final project, students each take on one of the roles of the design and production team. They hold mock production meetings to develop a cohesive design concept and to develop a production calendar. This course is a further development of 536 Choreographic Production and Design and is a requirement for students whose Thesis Project involves producing a concert. Graduate Dance majors only; instructor permission required; typically offered Fall, Winter

courses.title: Thesis 2: Proposal
courses.description: Following the students' Summer Research Project presentation, their next steps are to scope the Thesis proper and to select their Committee. A Thesis Chair should be determined by October 1 and the student should then meet with his/her Chair to discuss the overall design of the project. A Thesis Committee, comprising an additional Dance faculty member and a relevant expert from beyond the Department, should be determined by November 1 and a full proposal submitted to the Thesis Chair by December 1. The 3,000 word Thesis Proposal should include the following: a working title which articulates the research focus; project parameters and objectives; theoretical/practical perspective and proposed methodology; key research questions and/or issues; a critical review of the literature and other sources which will inform the research; a proposed timetable for the execution of the project; a budget (All Masters' students are eligible to apply for up to $1,200 to support their Thesis Project). Graduate Dance majors only; instructor permission required; typically offered Fall

courses.title: Thesis 3: Project
courses.description: The Thesis Project comprises three components. For MFA students, the Project must include a performative element, production work, and final written Documentation. A detailed account of course requirements, assessment criteria and submission guidelines are provided in the MFA Dance handbook. Graduate Dance majors only; instructor permission required

courses.title: Contemporary Basic Musicianship
courses.description: This course is the basic musicianship component to the course offerings from the theory department and will be the companion lab experience to Theory 139. There are essentially three components to this course: (1) ear-training audits (singing, dictation, and transcription), (2) rhythm audits, and (3) stylistic focus from each of the full-time members of the JCI faculty. Instructor permission required; typically offered Fall, Winter

courses.title: Roots Music and Improvisation
courses.description: Roots Music and Improvisation for students is a class for string players looking to continue to expand their musical growth into the realms of "Roots Music" - any non-classical tradition of acoustic string music, covering a vast range or genres of fiddle music: old-time, Celtic, bluegrass, new-grass, etc. Learn common "fiddle" repertoire, accompaniment skills, and genre-specific improvisation skills through the lenses of variation, ornamentation, and personal creative exploration.

courses.title: Jazz Styles and Historical Practice
courses.description: A survey of the history of jazz styles from its roots to contemporary practice. In addition to readings and listening projects, the course will also include hands-on learning of historical practice from classic and contemporary jazz. Additional goals include acquiring a deeper appreciation of the cultural and historical context and important terminology necessary to describe it casually. Instructor permission required.

courses.title: Black Music Matters
courses.description: The class explores Black American Music, its marginalized place in America's educational systems, notably music studies, and its creative, integrative and transformative tools for personal and collective growth. Instructor permission required.

courses.title: Portfolio and Career Development
courses.description: This course will examine and develop student projects for engagement as a working model for best professional practices. In addition to examining aesthetics, this course will also explore how to apply course work into the fabric of existing and future industry paradigms. Students are encouraged to develop projects in diverse musical settings for presentation beyond the classroom and graduation. Projects in mainstream jazz, contemporary improvisation, classical perspectives, soul, neo soul, hip hop, and other popular streams are encouraged. Instructor permission required.

courses.title: Contemplative Practice Seminar
courses.description: Explores contemplative disciplines through historical, theoretical perspectives, and through direct experience. Instructor permission required; typically offered Fall, Winter, Spring

courses.title: Special Topics
courses.description: The course considers various issues in aesthetics, pedagogy and cognition as related to jazz and contemporary improvised music. Typically offered Fall, Winter, Spring, Summer

courses.title: Creativity and Consciousness

In addition, the course will address beginning jazz pedagogy and will be helpful to Music Education students. Instructor permission required; typically offered Fall

courses.title: Compositional Forms
courses.description: Examine music compositions through a broad musical perspective. Composition will be explored through the optics of the composer, the performer, the composer/performer, and the audience. Furtherviews by musicologists, philosophers, and psychologists will provide an interdisciplinary lens to the topic. Historically established music traditions (e.g concert music and jazz) are contrasted with new forms (e.g. techno, hip-hop) in search of the expanding role of music composition. SMTD Jazz majors only; instructor permission required; typically offered Fall

courses.title: Jazz Arranging I
courses.description: Basic arranging techniques for medium-size jazz ensemble. SMTD Jazz majors only; instructor permission required; typically offered Fall

courses.title: Improvisational Forms
courses.description: Improvisation in eclectic style. Instructor permission required; typically offered Fall

courses.title: Upper Level Improvisation
courses.description: This course is the capstone improvisation course for the undergraduate degree in Jazz and Contemporary Improvisation. The course will examine expanded approaches to improvisation through repertoire, drills, and other devices to explore the theoretical, historical, philosophical, and aesthetic elements of improvisation. Topics include the cultivation of advanced melodic, motivic, harmonic, formal, textural and sonic skills. Exercises are designed to help students develop “in the moment” and analysis skills along with discussion and debate on the theory and practice of the learned materials.Prerequisite: JAZZ 467. SMTD Jazz majors only; instructor permission required; typically offered Fall, Winter

courses.title: Jazz Improvisation IV
courses.description: Experiential approach to the study of jazz improvisation. Prerequisite: JAZZ 471. SMTD Jazz majors only; instructor permission required; typically offered Winter

courses.title: Jazz Pedagogy
courses.description: This course will cover aspects of secondary school jazz pedagogy including improvisation, combo direction and large ensemble direction. Specific technique relevant to instruments typically used in jazz groups will be addressed as well, including trumpet, trombone, saxophone, piano, bass, guitar and drum set. Prerequisite: JAZZ 220, 221, or 462. Typically offered Fall

courses.title: Classroom Instruments
courses.description: This course is designed to provide prospective music teachers with the skills necessary to teach lessons using recorder, ukulele, guitar, unpitched percussion and barred instruments. Students will also be able to accompany songs with piano accompaniment. Typically offered Winter

courses.title: Teaching String Instruments I
courses.description: Presents pedagogy and techniques for teaching string instruments in an ensemble setting for certification degree requirements.Typically offered Fall

courses.title: Teaching String Instruments II
courses.description: Presents pedagogy and techniques for teaching string instruments in an ensemble setting for certification degree requirements. Typically offered Winter

courses.title: Wind and Percussion Techniques I
courses.description: Presents pedagogy techniques for teaching wind and percussion instruments in an ensemble setting for certification degree program. Typically offered Fall

courses.title: Wind and Percussion Techniques II
courses.description: Presents pedagogy techniques for teaching wind and percussion instruments in an ensemble setting for certification degree program. Typically offered Winter

courses.title: Special Topics
courses.description: Typically offered Fall, Winter

courses.title: Vocal Methods
courses.description: The vocal methods course is designed to provide prospective music educators with the skills to model and work effectively with students of all ages in a band/choral setting. The course content will include vocal instruction and topics related to vocal pedagogy. The setting will be that of a class with the former taught by a vocal GSI and the latter by the music education faculty and a music education GSI. Typically offered Winter

courses.title: Choral Techniques and Methods for Secondary Schools
courses.description: Introduces vocal techniques suitable for adolescent voices and effective rehearsal procedures. Examine music currently being used in secondary schools and criteria for selecting appropriate materials. Observation of school choirs is included. Prerequisite: CONDUCT 315; admission to the Teacher Certification Program. Instructor permission required; typically offered Winter

courses.title: Teaching General Music in Elementary Schools
courses.description: Presents materials and techniques for teaching general music to elementary students. Utilizes lectures, group discussion, peer teaching, readings, and demonstrations. Prerequisite: MUSED 131, PIANO 112; admission to the Teacher Certification Program. Instructor permission required; typically offered Fall

courses.title: Teaching General Music in Secondary Schools
courses.description: Introduces philosophies, objectives, materials, and organization of secondary general music classes. Utilizes lecture-demonstrations, peer teaching, readings, group discussion, and films. Prerequisite: PIANO 112; admission to the Teacher Certification Program. Instructor permission required; typically offered Winter

courses.title: Fundamentals of Teaching String Instruments
courses.description: Introduces philosophies, objectives, materials, and group methods for teaching string instruments in elementary and secondary schools. Prerequisite: MUSED 201, 202; admission to the Teacher Certification Program. Instructor permission required; typically offered Winter

courses.title: Elementary Band Methods
courses.description: Assists the student in developing the necessary skills for a position as an elementary or middle school band director. Topics include: recruitment, program organization and scheduling, building musicianship, materials for instruction, national standards, and state frameworks in instrumental music and classroom management. Prerequisite: MUSED 203, 205, 220; admission to the Teacher Certification Program. Instructor permission required; typically offered Winter

courses.title: Secondary Instrumental Methods
courses.description: Study and discussion of the role of the secondary instrumental music educator and the purpose of instrumental music in schools. Assists the student in developing the necessary skills for a position as an instrumental music teacher in the high school. Prerequisite: MUSED 203, 205, 220, CONDUCT 315; admission to the Teacher Certification Program. Instructor permission required; typically offered Fall

courses.title: Special Topics
courses.description: Typically offered Fall, Winter

courses.title: Music in Childhood
courses.description: Provides practical suggestions for teaching music skills to children. Students perform and learn to teach music. Typically offered Fall, Winter

courses.title: Teaching Private Lessons to Middle and High School Students
courses.description: Designed for music performance students who are preparing to teach private lessons. Topics include: musical development, movement, rhythm and rhythmic notation, aural skills and tonal notation, creative musicianship, musical sensitivity, preparing students for solo and ensemble, and logistics of private studio teaching. Typically offered Winter

courses.title: String Pedagogy I
courses.description: This course addresses the pedagogical skills for working effectively with beginning students in private lessons and group classes. Typically offered Fall

courses.title: String Pedagogy II
courses.description: This course addresses the pedagogical skills for working effectively with intermediate students in private lessons and group classes. Typically offered Winter

courses.title: Social Justice in the Performing Arts
courses.description: This course will examine the performing arts as they relate to issues of social justice. Important issues such as racism and anti-racism, intersectionality, identity, socioeconomic status, culturally responsive pedagogy, and reciprocal community engagement will be discussed, with a focus on how performing and teaching can better recognize and affirm identities and promote change.

courses.title: Community Engagement in Music Education
courses.description: 2-hour weekly seminar on campus and placement by Department of Music Education faculty in a community engagement setting. May be repeated for credit. Instructor permission required.

courses.title: Special Projects and Readings
courses.description: Instructor permission required; typically offered Fall, Winter

courses.title: Student Teaching
courses.description: Students in the Teacher Certification Program and whose application for student teaching has been accepted. Designed to provide practical experience and to develop teaching skills through observation and teaching in K-12 schools under joint supervision of university and school personnel. Elected concurrently with MUSED 496; instructor permission required; typically offered Fall, Winter

courses.title: Seminar
courses.description: Weekly campus seminar, providing a setting for reflection and further engagement about the practice of teaching and learning. Elected concurrently with MUSED 495; instructor permission required; typically offered Fall, Winter

courses.title: Educational Research in the Arts
courses.description: Study of research processes in schools and communities, with an emphasis on framing problems and evaluating studies, drawing on diverse modes of inquiry. Typically offered Fall, Summer

courses.title: Psychology of Music Teaching and Learning
courses.description: Study of the psychological foundations of music teaching and learning, including perception, motivation, creative and critical thinking, and musical development. Typically offered Winter, Summer

courses.title: Music, Society, and Education
courses.description: Study of music's role in society and education from historical and philosophical perspectives. Instructor permission required; typically offered Fall, Summer

courses.title: Teaching and Learning in the Arts
courses.description: Draws upon related foundational disciplines to examine teaching and learning in group and individual instructional settings. This course addresses topics related to curriculum theory, instructional innovations and assessment strategies. Instructor permission required; typically offered Winter, Summer

courses.title: Teaching Music in Higher Education
courses.description: Includes an examination of theories of music teaching and learning, adult learning styles, developmental stages experienced by undergraduate students, and discussions of issues in the teaching of music in higher education. Typically offered Fall

courses.description: Study of the music education research literature with an emphasis on framing research problems and evaluating research studies from a wide range or research traditions. Typically offered Winter

courses.description: Required for all doctoral students during the first four semesters. Bi-weekly seminar involving faculty, students, and invited guests in presentations of their research work at various stages of completion. Instructor permission required; typically offered Fall, Winter

courses.title: Research in Music Education II
courses.description: Continued study of music education research literature with emphasis on the creation of original, defensible proposals for doctoral dissertation. Typically offered Winter

courses.title: Seminar in Music Teacher Education
courses.description: Examination of research and models of instruction in music teacher education with an emphasis on the teaching of undergraduate methods courses in instrumental, choral, and/or general music. Typically offered Fall

courses.title: Introduction to Guitar
courses.description: A hands-on introduction to guitar performance, including basic instrumental technique, instrument care, music literacy, and performance styles. No previous experience necessary.

courses.title: Introduction to Songwriting
courses.description: This introductory course in popular songwriting includes a survey of diverse and iconic songwriters throughout popular music history and will teach students myriad creative skills to compose original pop songs through fun and collaborative songwriting projects. This class is designed to nurture student songwriting in a supportive classroom environment as we strive to illuminate songwriting fundamentals, define personal vision, and expand artistic boundaries. Course work will include: a survey of songwriting examples from different decades and genres of popular music to learn songwriting techniques, prompts for constructing melodies and harmonic progressions, lyric analysis, exploring song arrangement, and discussing the power of a song for social commentary and self expression. No prior songwriting experience necessary!

courses.title: Songwriting Workshop
courses.description: This course nurtures folk and pop songwriting in a supportive workshop environment. New songs will be performed and critiqued as we strive to deepen understanding of songwriting techniques, expand our expressive boundaries, and discover our collective and personal artistic mission.

courses.title: Introduction to Rap Songwriting
courses.description: This course introduces the fundamentals of rap songwriting and spoken word performance. Areas of focus include message, intentionality, form, and style. Students will be encouraged to explore their own artistic voice. No previous musical experience is required.

courses.title: Rap Songwriting Workshop
courses.description: This course nurtures rap songwriting in a supportive workshop environment. New songs will be performed and critiqued as we strive to deepen understanding of rap songwriting techniques, expand our expressive boundaries, and discover our collective and personal artistic mission.

courses.title: BA Music Forum
courses.description: Seminar for music BA students to explore contemporary issues in the musical arts and related fields. Topics include arts leadership, the music industry, research and writing, community engagement, arts activism, and additional topics generated by the class.

courses.title: Honors Seminar
courses.description: This interactive seminar assists students in developing an undergraduate honors project or thesis. Students gain research, analytical, grant writing, and project management skills while focused on an independent capstone project.

courses.title: Honors Thesis
courses.description: Updated 3/27/26

courses.title: Introduction to the Art of Music
courses.description: Introduces western music for the listener in overview from the baroque era to the present.This course offers an introduction to Western art music (also known as classical music) from 1700 to the present. Students will gain fluency in describing the elements of music (musical forms and styles, aesthetics, instruments, and genres) in addition to learning how historical and societal developments have influenced music over time. The course will introduce students to works by composers such as Bach, Beethoven, and Stravinsky. Students will also learn about lesser-known composers, such as Joseph Bologne, Clara Schumann, and William Grant Still, who have been marginalized, often because of their race or gender. Through listening, reading, discussing, and attending live concerts, students will learn how to think critically and communicate effectively about classical music. Non-SMTD students only; typically offered Winter

courses.title: Introduction to World Music
courses.description: This course introduces students to world music cultures through the lens of anthropology and ethnomusicology. It foregrounds the study of music in the context of culture. Emphasizing the question of music’s meaning, we will analyze selected musical cultures in North and South America, Asia, Europe, and Africa. We will critically engage with the ways in which religious, political, and economic factors shape the identities and behaviors of performers and listeners. Positioning varying music traditions within a broader context of postcolonial as well as technological and transnational development, we will pay close attention to the ever-changing balance between traditional and modern ideas of music and musicking – in systems of learning, performance as well as approaches to writing and recording music. No prior music background is required to take this course.

courses.title: Introduction to Popular Music
courses.description: In this introductory course, we will explore the artistry and business of popular music from 1900 to the present day. Students will be asked to consider their own musical experiences and histories as we study the ways popular music interfaces with economics, technology, politics, and social movements throughout the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. Designed to develop listening and analytical skills, the course aims to help you understand, describe, interpret, and write about popular music. Non-SMTD students only; typically offered Fall

courses.title: Opera!
courses.description: Opera is a collaborative art form, bringing together poets, scenographers, musicians, choreographers, singers and dancers. It was invented in the late Renaissance by a select group of Florentine intellectuals who sought to enhance the emotional power of theater. Since then, opera has remained an extravagant art and a spectacle of considerable force used as a catalyst for reflecting on what it means to be human, to perceive and to experience. This introductory-level course to opera explores a repertory of exceeding beauty and interest while it considers this form of theater as a fold for thinking about the value of song, empathy, myth, beauty, and the politics of entertainment in the world in which we live. This is an introductory course; no previous knowledge of opera is required, only a desire to listen to opera and study it. Non-SMTD students only; typically offered Winter

courses.title: Introduction to the Study of Music
courses.description: A survey of musical concepts and repertories of the Western and non-Western world. This course introduces students to some of the fundamental, yet diverse topics, theories, and methods in ethno(musicology). It is neither a historical nor a music theory course but rather a topical-approach course that explores various interdisciplinary intersections among the fields of ethnomusicology, musicology, music theory, psychology, sociology, anthropology, phenomenology, music acoustics, and philosophy. The goal of the course is to unveil disciplinary intersectionality and, thus, nurture a well-rounded experience of learning musicology. Through weekly lectures, readings, discussions, and listening examples, students will experience the study of music as a global, as well as human, and nonhuman phenomenon. They will develop skills of writing a college-level paper about music, and music in culture, and learn how to read and critically engage with assigned scholarly works. By developing a vocabulary for understanding and describing music, and exploring selected frameworks that musicologists employ, students will learn how to listen to, and analyze unfamiliar music through a music-cultural lens. SMTD students only; typically offered Fall

courses.title: History of US Musics
courses.description: This is a survey-style course intended to familiarize students with the history of American music. Though there will be moments of taking a longer view of American musical history, we will focus primarily on developments from the 19th century to the present. A key component of this work will be understanding how these musics and the individuals who created and engaged with them influenced and were influenced by their social, political, and cultural environments. Along the way we will remain attentive to the ways that both personal and national identities have and continue to inflect American musical cultures across time and space. Full class meetings consist of a combination of lecture, discussion, and group listening. Students will also be expected to attend weekly discussion sections. SMTD students only; typically offered Winter

courses.title: History of Music
courses.description: History of music from the Middle Ages through the Baroque. The course is conceived as a journey through European music from the Middle Ages through the mid- 18th-century. Students will acquire familiarity with the musical styles, genres, and aesthetic priorities of the Medieval, Renaissance, and Baroque periods, against the backdrop of the social and political context in which this music was composed, performed, and heard. Our overarching goal is to learn how to dialogue with history by interrogating the musical choices from centuries ago in the light of the aesthetic and social values of the time, as well as their significance to Western musical culture of the modern era. SMTD students only; typically offered Fall

courses.title: History of Western Music
courses.description: An examination of the music of the Western classical tradition from the mid-eighteenth century into the twentieth century. Students will gain a framework for approaching music of this tradition as performers and students, and they will develop a critical stance toward it. SMTD students only; typically offered Winter

courses.title: Music and Islam
courses.description: This course focuses on the unity and diversity of musical customs from the Muslim cultures of the Middle East, Central Asia, north India and Indonesia. We will investigate musical systems in terms of instruments, repertoire, modal and rhythmic structures and the effect of religious constraints, cultural policy and social history on musical life. Non-SMTD students only; typically offered Fall

courses.title: History of Music
courses.description: An introduction to European music from the Middle Ages to the mid 18th century for undergraduate students. The course pursues two related objectives: on the one hand, it aims at leading students to acquire familiarity with the basic musical forms, styles, and structures of the pre-modern era. On the other hand, it reflects on the role and significance of music in relation to contemporaneous issues of power structures, race and gender dynamics, and coloniality. Basic familiarity with the rudiments of music and musical notation will be helpful, but it is not required. Non-SMTD students only; typically offered Fall

courses.title: History of Music
courses.description: Non-SMTD students only; typically offered Winter Sections for Fall 2026 MUSICOL 346.001: From the Eighteenth Century to the Present Tuesday/Thursday 1:00 - 2:30 pm BMT 506 Prof. Stefano Mengozzi

courses.title: Early History of Opera
courses.description: In this course, students will think critically about opera as a theatrical and literary art form, a live performance medium, and a mode of cultural expression during the 17th and 18th centuries. We will consider operas from Monteverdi to Mozart and examine the implications of performing this repertoire in the present. A special focus of this course will be on the intersections between opera, politics, and power. How did composers use opera as a medium for political commentary? In what ways were operas interpreted as political in their own time and well beyond? Students will explore these questions by engaging closely with primary sources, scholarship from the disciplines of musicology, history, and literary studies, and by watching various stagings of operatic productions.

courses.title: 19th - 20th Century Opera
courses.description: An historical survey of opera (as music, as theater, and as cultural expression) from the 19th century through the present. A history of opera after 1800, addressing the entanglement of the artform with Western modernity. The course centers on the study of a chosen repertory, exploring the ways in which operatic music and song function as significant media for the articulation of subjectivity, gender, identity, as well as history, memory, morality, truth, myth, music itself, and the value of art.Typically offered Winter

courses.title: History of Jazz
courses.description: Surveys jazz in the United States from its beginnings in African-American aural traditions to the present. In this course, we will examine the history and development of jazz music from its origins in the late nineteenth century to the present. Throughout, we will explore how the music and musicians both influence and are influenced by contemporaneous social, cultural, and political developments. Building upon the greater scholarly and critical attention given to musicians’ identities, politics, and cultural backgrounds since the 1990s and the inception of the “New Jazz Studies” we will remain attentive throughout to historiographical practices that shape the ways we do, or do not, know jazz music and its history. Course meetings will consist of a combination of lecture, discussion, and group listening. Typically offered Winter

courses.title: Topics in Baroque Music
courses.description: This course, designed for advanced undergraduates and graduate students, is devoted to the study of European (and some colonial Latin American) music from the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. Music is to be studied critically, as music and as culture. Assignments will be primarily listening assignments, supplemented by score study, readings from materials on reserve, and some in-class performances. Typically offered Winter

courses.title: Music of the Classic Era
courses.description: A survey of European music of the 17th and early 18th centuries. Typically offered Fall

courses.title: 20th Century Music
courses.description: A survey of Western music since about 1900. The twentieth century witnessed profound changes to how Western classical music was composed, performed, and consumed. To explore these transformations, we will examine topics such as the impact of new technologies on music-making, the rise of multi-art performances, and the relation between Western-trained musicians and the non-Western world. Along the way, we will study compositions by well-established figures (such as Paul Hindemith, Steve Reich, and Erik Satie), as well as those whose place in the concert hall is less secure (such as Julius Eastman, Nadia Boulanger, and Unsuk Chin). This is a discussion-based course and students are expected to actively participate in course meetings. To hone skills in listening to and thinking about music, students will read academic articles, study scores, and complete both formal and informal written assignments. Prerequisite: MUSICOL 240. Typically offered Fall

courses.title: The Art Song
courses.description: A survey of European and American art song of the 19th and 20th centuries. Typically offered Fall

courses.title: Music in the U.S.
courses.description: A lecture survey of American music from the 18th century to the present, including both formal and informal traditions.Typically offered Fall

courses.title: Music of Black Americans
courses.description: An explication of the development of the Afro-American musical traditions from African and Afro-American folk origins to Black American music in the twentieth century. Topics include blues, jazz, contemporary popular music, and art music.Typically offered Fall

courses.title: Music in Culture
courses.description: Culture is sometimes defined simply as a people’s way of life or as the combination of shared beliefs and practices. Despite the title of this course, however, music doesn’t only exist within culture; it also shapes, maintains, performs, and changes culture. Most importantly, culture is holistic, shared, and is part of how people understand themselves in relation to others. In this class we will use case studies from many communities of the United States as launching points to explore music as culture in collective identity-making processes. Considering time, place, and other factors, how is music integral to social life? In what ways can shared beliefs and practices of music connect people not only locally, but also nationally and transnationally?

courses.title: Music of Latin American & Caribbean
courses.description: In this course, we explore a diverse range of Latin American and Caribbean music, mainly from the 1950s to contemporary times. We will examine well-known genres such as Brazilian bossa nova and baile funk, reggae and dancehall, salsa, and reggaeton, alongside less obvious but influential styles like Columbian cumbia, Peruvian chicha, and the international impact of Brazilian metal band Sepultura. Throughout the course, the Afro-diasporic and Indigenous aspects of these musics will be central to our exploration, highlighting their vital contributions to the cultural and musical landscapes of the region. We will also touch upon key figures who bridged popular and classical traditions, such as Guerra Peixe, whose compositions and teachings incorporated Brazilian popular music into classical frameworks, enriching both worlds. The course focuses on Latin America and Caribbean urban musics, which have played a significant role in shaping international musical and cultural scenes. By the end of the course, students will be equipped to properly understand, analyze, and write about Latin American and Caribbean music. They will also be able to critically examine how these musics connect to and influence popular culture in the United States.

courses.title: Music of Africa
courses.description: This course explores the rich musical traditions of Africa through in-depth reading as well as close listening and/or viewing of assigned weekly examples. While this is not a survey course, we will explore and scrutinize some of the “issues” and content about instruments (including voice, music styles, genres, as well as contexts) that give rise to the production and consumption of music within particular histories and socio-political settings in Africa and in some instances, within the African diaspora. To enhance a critical reflection upon the multiple perspectives on music in Africa (including North Africa and the sub-Saharan region of the continent), we will draw on an ethnomusicological approach – the study of music in the context of culture.

courses.title: Music of the Middle East, India, and Southeast Asia
courses.description: In this course, we will study the classical and light-classical forms of North Indian music. Along with an explication of the melodic and rhythmic systems, instruments, and performance genres,we will critically engage with some socio-cultural aspects of this tradition, focusing on themes such as embodiment and subjectivity-formation in training, transmission, and performance, and delving into issues of gender, caste, class, and religion. Through listening, reading, discussion, writing, and analysis, we will gain technical knowledge as well as an understanding of this music in its historical, socio-cultural, and political dimensions.

courses.title: Medieval Music
courses.description: A survey of European music from the Middle Ages to about 1420. Typically offered Fall

courses.title: Independent Study
courses.description: SMTD students only; offered Fall, Winter

courses.title: Introduction to Graduate Study
courses.description: This course introduces the methods, discourse, and intellectual debates animating the study of music history today. Questions addressed will include: How did the discipline of musicology, with its Germanic roots, make a transition to the United States? What are the assumptions (and biases) upon which musicological discourse rests in the last thirty years? To what extent and purpose do music historians draw on intellectual concerns, critical paradigms, and research strategies from related disciplines? What is the relevance of our discipline in today’s world, whether in the academy, the diverse worlds of musical performance, or to the publics of today? Alongside the study of these questions, students will develop their portfolios of research-based activities, developing expertise in current techniques of musicological and humanistic study, and, among others, honing their skills in archival investigation, the analysis of sources and texts, the interpretation of culture, historical narration and critical argumentation. Student portfolios will feature a variety of research exercises covering a broad spectrum of musicological techniques to be developed in the context of each student’s particular interest. For instance, each student will be asked to select a special research area they will track throughout the semester in dialogue with weekly readings about the discipline and its practices. Class periods will be run as seminars, and students should come to these meetings prepared to engage in thoughtful discussions of the weekly assigned literature and topics. At the same time, they work on their portfolio of research-based activities. SMTD students only; offered Fall, Winter

courses.title: Research Techniques
courses.description: This seminar offers graduate students in ethnomusicology and musicology practical exercises to develop their research, writing, and presentation skills. Class members will read current and seminal writings in ethno/musicology, write critical reviews and ethnographic reports on topics of their choices, conduct individualized field-work research projects, and prepare a number of formal and informal presentations. Graduate Musicology students only; typically offered Winter

courses.title: Music Bibliography
courses.description: This course introduces graduate students outside of the musicology department to the use of scholarly sources, citational practice, and other elements of academic research, with a focus on critically evaluating secondary literature. Other topics include historiography, evaluating constructs like the canon, handling controversial subjects, and writing for general versus specialized audiences. The final project is a research paper on a topic of students’ own choosing.

courses.title: Teaching an Introduction to Music
courses.description: A course in designing and teaching an Introduction to Music course for non-majors. In-class teaching practice is included. Musicologists teach in and out of classrooms, for different audiences, for various levels of understanding, and for a multitude of reasons. This course revolves around teaching musicology at the university level but keeps at the forefront the development of pedagogical skills for engaging wider and diverse audiences in other settings. The course integrates theoretical and practical readings, explores various instructional strategies, and offers students hands-on experience with designing courses, syllabi, assignments, and classroom activities; leading and participating in discussions; and reflecting and writing about the challenges of teaching. Students should expect to prepare and deliver in-class teaching presentations throughout the semester. Typically offered Fall

To hone skills in listening to and thinking about music, students will read academic articles, study scores, and complete both formal and informal written assignments. Prerequisite: MUSICOL 240. Typically offered Fall

courses.title: The Art Song
courses.description: A survey of European and American art song of the 19th and 20th centuries. Typically offered Fall

courses.title: Introduction to Ethnomusicology
courses.description: This course is an introductory foray into the scholarly and sonic world of ethnomusicology. A relatively young field, since its inception ethnomusicology has strived to self-reflexively improve its approach and purview as a humanities discipline. This has led to a constant development of new themes and areas of study. Our course will focus on some of these. We will begin with a broad history of scholarship in ethnomusicology, and then move to a consideration of specific issues, such as: What is gained, and what lost, if we expand our consideration of music to the broader category of sound? How does attention to music as an affective practice elucidate the process of meaning and knowledge making? How have ethnomusicologists addressed issues relating to identity such as race, religion, nation, gender, and sexuality? Our discussions will be in relation to a variety of musical cultures from around the globe, emphasizing the discipline’s openness to repertories studied. Over the course of the semester, we will get a sense of ethnomusicology also as an inherently interdisciplinary and people-centric field of study.

courses.title: Music in the U.S.
courses.description: A lecture survey of American music from the 18th century to the present, including both formal and informal traditions.Typically offered Fall

courses.title: Music of Black Americans
courses.description: An explication of the development of the Afro-American musical traditions from African and Afro-American folk origins to Black American music in the twentieth century. Topics include blues, jazz, contemporary popular music, and art music.Typically offered Fall

courses.title: Music in Culture
courses.description: Culture is sometimes defined simply as a people’s way of life or as the combination of shared beliefs and practices. Despite the title of this course, however, music doesn’t only exist within culture; it also shapes, maintains, performs, and changes culture. Most importantly, culture is holistic, shared, and is part of how people understand themselves in relation to others. In this class we will use case studies from many communities of the United States as launching points to explore music as culture in collective identity-making processes. Considering time, place, and other factors, how is music integral to social life? In what ways can shared beliefs and practices of music connect people not only locally, but also nationally and transnationally?

courses.title: Music of Latin American & Caribbean
courses.description: In this course, we explore a diverse range of Latin American and Caribbean music, mainly from the 1950s to contemporary times. We will examine well-known genres such as Brazilian bossa nova and baile funk, reggae and dancehall, salsa, and reggaeton, alongside less obvious but influential styles like Columbian cumbia, Peruvian chicha, and the international impact of Brazilian metal band Sepultura. Throughout the course, the Afro-diasporic and Indigenous aspects of these musics will be central to our exploration, highlighting their vital contributions to the cultural and musical landscapes of the region. We will also touch upon key figures who bridged popular and classical traditions, such as Guerra Peixe, whose compositions and teachings incorporated Brazilian popular music into classical frameworks, enriching both worlds. The course focuses on Latin America and Caribbean urban musics, which have played a significant role in shaping international musical and cultural scenes. By the end of the course, students will be equipped to properly understand, analyze, and write about Latin American and Caribbean music. They will also be able to critically examine how these musics connect to and influence popular culture in the United States.

courses.title: Music of Africa
courses.description: This course explores the rich musical traditions of Africa through in-depth reading as well as close listening and/or viewing of assigned weekly examples. While this is not a survey course, we will explore and scrutinize some of the “issues” and content about instruments (including voice, music styles, genres, as well as contexts) that give rise to the production and consumption of music within particular histories and socio-political settings in Africa and in some instances, within the African diaspora. To enhance a critical reflection upon the multiple perspectives on music in Africa (including North Africa and the sub-Saharan region of the continent), we will draw on an ethnomusicological approach – the study of music in the context of culture.

courses.title: Music of the Middle East, India, and Southeast Asia
courses.description: In this course, we will study the classical and light-classical forms of North Indian music. Along with an explication of the melodic and rhythmic systems, instruments, and performance genres,we will critically engage with some socio-cultural aspects of this tradition, focusing on themes such as embodiment and subjectivity-formation in training, transmission, and performance, and delving into issues of gender, caste, class, and religion. Through listening, reading, discussion, writing, and analysis, we will gain technical knowledge as well as an understanding of this music in its historical, socio-cultural, and political dimensions.

courses.title: History of Music Theory I
courses.description: This course is designed to give graduate students an overview of the main trajectories in musical thought from Classical Antiquity to the early 18th century. The broad time span will enable us to observe the rise and fall of select doctrines, concepts, and terminologies through time, in the context of evolving historical circumstances. Does music theory change primarily in response to the evolution of musical practice, or rather as a result of ongoing debates and reflections upon musical phenomena internal to the discipline? A second key question, that will likely loom large in our class discussions throughout the semester is that of the ontological vs. epistemological status of music theory, more precisely: do the acts of theorizing and naming musical objects affect the ontology of those objects, or should they rather be viewed, more mundanely, as mere ways of knowing those objects? What is at stake in the answer to that question? SMTD graduate students only

courses.description: This seminar examines current issues and practices of historicizing music from local, national, and global perspectives. It will consist of two tracks: an intensive reading and discussion of current publications on the topic and detailed case studies on music and music cultures selected by seminar participants. As writing exercises, students will develop historical narratives about the music and compositions they are studying and performing. courses.title: Early Renaissance Music
courses.description: As “tonal” listeners, how do we make sense of a “pre-tonal,” though often tonal-sounding repertory? How do we reconcile the conceptual foundations of 15 th - and 16 th -century music with our inescapable 21 st -century modes of listening, shaped at least in part by the values, theories, and aesthetics of the intervening centuries? To what extent is it possible to develop a “historically informed” musical ear, and is it desirable to do so? How do we strike the thoughtful balance between presentist and historicist approaches to early music advocated by some scholars? Seeking to find answers to such questions, the seminar will take a close look at diatonic theory of the Renaissance era vis-à-vis modern theories of tonality, while assessing the merit of various music-analytic methodologies that have been proposed in the last few decades.

courses.description: This course provides students credit for performance in opera productions. By audition. Students must have achieved Upper-Level Standing in Voice to be eligible to audition. Instructor permission required. Typically offered Fall, Winter

courses.title: Recitative
courses.description: This class is designed to deepen and sharpen opera performance skills for advanced-intermediate and advanced singers by focusing on Italian Recitative from a range of composers and time periods in both the secco and accompagnato styles. By the end of this course, students will understand best practices for thorough recitative preparation, coaching, and nuanced performing. Proficiency in Italian diction required to enroll.
